headline: US markets rallied last night with NASDAQ up 1.25%, MSFT surged to $501 on AI momentum, while back home PLS slipped 2.65% as major banks now tip a November rate hike.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft jumped 1.07% last night to $501.68 USD, riding a wave of enthusiasm for AI infrastructure plays. Billionaire Bill Ackman was reported to be buying MSFT stock, and retail investors have it flagged as a top AI infrastructure pick. The narrative around Microsoft being the pick-up-the-shovel play in the AI gold rush continues to drive the price higher.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS fell 2.65% today to $5.15, giving back some of recent gains. Despite a strong headline — lithium prices are reportedly up 92% year-over-year and PLS Group posted a A$526M profit — the stock is still well off its highs and sentiment remains nervous. The looming prospect of an RBA rate hike in November is also broadly weighing on risk assets like mining stocks.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slipped 1.05% last night to $231.00 USD. The slide came despite genuinely positive news — GTA VI pre-orders are reportedly at 'eye-watering' levels and there's talk of a GTA VI deal with Netflix. The dip looks like general profit-taking rather than anything structural; the GTA VI story remains a major long-term catalyst.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google dipped a modest 0.36% last night to $337.89 USD. There was no major negative catalyst — it's likely just some rotation toward Microsoft, which drew more attention as the 'preferred AI infrastructure play' in commentary overnight. The long-term AI story for Alphabet remains intact, with Gemini 3.5 also launching a new speech-to-text model this week.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: No price data available for today's ASX close — VDHG didn't trade or data wasn't captured. Previous close was $77.22. As a broadly diversified high-growth ETF, it tracks global and Australian equities, so last night's strong US session is a tailwind heading into the next trading day.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: No price data for today's ASX close. Previous close was $525.98. VTS tracks the entire US share market, so last night's solid S&P 500 (+0.59%) and NASDAQ (+1.25%) session bodes well for the next print.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: No price data for today's ASX close. Previous close was $93.61. Emerging markets continue to face headwinds from a firmer AUD and global uncertainty around the Iran conflict, though the AUD/USD tick higher of 0.44% last night is a mild positive for overseas returns.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: No price data for today's ASX close. Previous close was $16.09. The AI ETF theme remains very much alive — with MSFT surging on AI momentum and Google launching new speech-to-text capabilities via Gemini 3.5, the underlying theme is strong even if today's price wasn't updated.

watch_today.title: Rate hike coming in November — RBA watch is on
watch_today.detail: ANZ and CBA have both shifted their forecasts and are now tipping an RBA interest rate hike in November, after July's inflation data came in higher than expected and household spending rose strongly. Three of the Big Four banks now agree a hike is coming. This matters for your portfolio — higher rates generally weigh on growth stocks and risk assets, including PLS. Keep an eye on any RBA commentary in coming weeks.

watch_today.title: MSFT — strong AI momentum, sitting on a 13% gain
watch_today.detail: Microsoft jumped another 1.07% last night to $501.68, and you're now up 13.22% on your position (about $51 AUD profit). Bill Ackman buying MSFT and the AI infrastructure narrative are both tailwinds. For a long-term holder, this is a hold — nothing suggests selling. If you're thinking of topping up, the story is as strong as ever.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — down 2.65% today, but lithium fundamentals are improving
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals fell to $5.15 today, and you're sitting on a 23.59% loss on this position (about -$35 AUD). That said, the underlying news is actually turning: lithium prices are up 92% year-on-year and PLS Group just posted a A$526M profit. The dip today looks like broader risk-off sentiment ahead of a potential RBA rate hike, not a change in the company's story. Sit tight — the long-term thesis is improving.

watch_today.title: TTWO — GTA VI hype is real, dip is noise
watch_today.detail: Take-Two slipped 1.05% last night despite genuinely bullish GTA VI news — pre-orders at 'eye-watering' levels and a possible Netflix distribution deal in play. You're very slightly in the red (-$3.24 AUD, -0.51%), but the long-term case here is the GTA VI release cycle, which is looking stronger by the week. Hold comfortably.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — AI theme firing on all cylinders
watch_today.detail: No price print today for GXAI, but the AI ETF theme is getting strong support: over 100 companies including OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic called for urgent action on AI safety (keeping AI regulation front-of-mind for investors), and Google launched a new Gemini 3.5 speech-to-text model. Long-term, this ETF is well-positioned. Hold and watch.

watch_today.title: US markets open tonight — NASDAQ on a roll
watch_today.detail: Last night the NASDAQ surged 1.25% to 26,457 and the S&P 500 gained 0.59% to 7,721. US markets open again tonight at ~11:30 PM AEST. With oil up 2.38% (to $84.19 — partly on Iran war tensions) and gold up 1.33% to $4,659, there's some inflation anxiety bubbling. Worth keeping an eye on tonight's session given the rate hike fears.

world.summary: The biggest global stories today centre on the six-month mark of the Iran war, an escalating legal battle over Trump's mail voting restrictions in the US, and a wave of global tech companies calling for urgent action on AI safety risks.

stories.title: Six months into the Iran war: regional powers scrambling for an exit
stories.why_it_matters: It's now been six months since the Iran war began, and Reuters has published a major assessment of what's changed. The conflict has had serious knock-on effects — oil prices have spiked (WTI crude is up 2.38% to $84.19 last night, partly due to ongoing Middle East instability), and regional powers are now actively seeking off-ramps to stop the fighting. The Council on Foreign Relations bluntly concluded the US has 'no good options.' For everyday Australians, higher oil prices feed directly into petrol costs and inflation — exactly the wrong environment when the RBA is already eyeing rate hikes.

stories.title: Trump's mail voting crackdown hits a legal wall — then keeps going anyway
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration has rolled out new rules tied to a presidential executive order that restrict mail ballot access — effectively making it harder to vote by post in parts of the US. A federal judge ruled the administration violated a court order by pushing ahead with the plan, but the US Postal Service confirmed the rules are now in effect regardless. The standoff between courts and the executive branch over voting rights is deepening ahead of future US elections, raising serious questions about democratic norms that analysts say could affect market stability and US governance confidence globally.

stories.title: 100+ tech giants — including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic — demand urgent action on rogue AI
stories.why_it_matters: More than 100 technology companies — including OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic — have signed a joint statement calling for urgent government action to defend against 'rogue AI' threats. This is a significant moment: the very companies building the most powerful AI systems are publicly admitting the risks could spiral without guardrails. The call is for governments to act now before the technology outpaces any regulatory response. For investors holding AI-exposed stocks (GOOG, MSFT, GXAI), this signals that regulation is coming — which could be a speed bump for growth but also lends long-term credibility to the sector.

stories.title: Meta agrees to $17 billion settlement — AI regulation debate explodes
stories.why_it_matters: Meta has agreed to a staggering $17 billion settlement — one of the largest in tech history — in a case that is being held up as a key example of why AI regulation cannot wait. The settlement has reignited calls from lawmakers and experts to regulate AI before it causes similarly large-scale harms. This is the backdrop behind the 100-company joint statement above. For anyone with tech or AI exposure in their portfolio, this is a reminder that regulatory risk is real and growing — but it also suggests big tech companies are now actively trying to get ahead of it rather than resist it.

markets.summary: Last night was a solid session in the US — the NASDAQ gained 1.25% and the S&P 500 was up 0.59%, driven by AI and tech momentum (particularly Microsoft). Oil jumped 2.38% to $84.19 on ongoing Middle East tensions from the Iran war. Gold pushed to $4,659 (+1.33%), reflecting uncertainty. The Aussie dollar nudged up 0.44% to 72 US cents. ASX 200 data wasn't available for today's close.

indicators.note: Solid gain last night — broad US market remains in good health, lifted by tech.

politics.summary: The big domestic story today is the growing consensus among Australia's major banks that an RBA interest rate hike is coming in November. Rising household spending and a surprise inflation result in July have the Reserve Bank in a difficult spot. Also, Albanese has backed down on a push to require AI data centres to run on renewable energy.

stories.title: ANZ and CBA now both tipping a November rate hike — three of the Big Four agree
stories.why_it_matters: CBA economists have shifted their forecast and now expect the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia — the body that sets interest rates) to raise rates at the November meeting, following a surprise jump in July's inflation data and strong household spending figures. ANZ agrees. That's three of the Big Four banks on the same page. A rate hike means mortgage repayments go up for anyone on a variable rate, and it typically slows consumer spending. For investors, it's a headwind for growth and risk assets — watch for broader ASX weakness in the lead-up.

stories.title: Rising household spending puts pressure on Labor and the RBA
stories.why_it_matters: Australians are spending more, not less — which sounds like good news but is actually complicating the inflation fight. The AFR reports this is putting pressure on both the Labor government (which wants to be seen as helping with cost of living) and the RBA (which needs to cool spending to bring inflation down). The bind: cutting rates too soon risks reigniting inflation; holding or hiking risks hurting households already under financial stress.

stories.title: Australia's federation is 'not working' — GST, gambling, gun buybacks all stuck
stories.why_it_matters: A piece in The Conversation today argues Australia's federal-state system is fundamentally broken — pointing to GST reform, online gambling regulation, and gun buyback policy as examples where states and the federal government can't get on the same page. For everyday Australians, this means sensible national policy on issues like gambling harm and firearms keeps getting stuck in political gridlock. It's a broader governance issue but relevant as Labor tries to deliver reform ahead of the next election cycle.

stories.title: Albanese backs down on renewable energy mandate for AI data centres
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government has dropped its push to force states to power AI data centres using renewable energy sources. The policy would have required that the massive electricity demand from AI computing infrastructure be met with clean energy. The backdown is seen as a win for the tech industry but a loss for Australia's renewable energy transition. Given Australia is trying to attract major tech investment (data centres mean jobs and economic activity), this tension between climate goals and economic development is likely to keep coming up.

ai.summary: Today's AI news has a clear theme: the industry is confronting its own risks head-on. Over 100 companies signed a joint call for urgent action on AI threats, a new Gemini 3.5 speech-to-text model launched, and the debate around AI regulation is intensifying globally.

stories.title: 100+ companies — OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and more — call for urgent action on rogue AI
stories.why_it_matters: In a rare show of unity, over 100 AI companies — including the biggest names in the industry (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) — have jointly called on governments to act urgently against the threat of 'rogue AI': AI systems that operate outside human control or are deliberately weaponised. This is notable because these companies are effectively saying 'please regulate us before things go wrong.' The statement signals the industry knows it is at an inflection point. For investors, this is both a risk flag (regulation is coming) and a reassurance (the big players are trying to shape sensible rules rather than fight them).

stories.title: Google Gemini 3.5 launches new speech-to-text AI model
stories.why_it_matters: Google has released a speech-to-text model as part of its Gemini 3.5 AI suite. In plain English: this means Gemini can now accurately convert spoken words to written text in real time, at a high level of quality. This kind of capability underpins voice assistants, transcription tools, live captions, and accessibility features. It's a direct shot at competitors like OpenAI's Whisper. For your GOOG holding, this is a reminder that Google is actively shipping new AI features — it's not just watching from the sidelines.

stories.title: AI influencers and actors in ads — may already be breaking the law
stories.why_it_matters: If you've seen an ad recently where the 'person' promoting a product looks a little too perfect, they may well be an AI-generated influencer or digital actor. Mashable reports that in many jurisdictions this is already technically illegal — advertising standards typically require disclosure when a human likeness is artificial. As AI-generated video and imagery becomes indistinguishable from real people, regulators around the world are scrambling to catch up. This is a practical issue that affects everyday consumers and brands alike.

stories.title: Meta's $17 billion settlement reignites the AI regulation debate
stories.why_it_matters: Meta's agreement to a $17 billion settlement (one of the largest tech settlements in history) is being used by advocates as a rallying cry: regulate AI now, before damage is done at scale. AI expert Amba Kak appeared on Democracy Now arguing that the same dynamics enabling large-scale harm in social media are already present in AI systems, and governments are falling behind. For investors, it's a signal that big tech regulatory risk is not going away — Meta's settlement is likely just the opening act.

sport.summary: Round 26 NRL is underway — the Storm demolished the Broncos 46-20 at Suncorp last night, which is a big result for the Gold Coast faithful to digest. The AFL finals picture is crystallising, the Matildas are drawing huge crowds, and the US Open tennis is building momentum.

stories.title: Storm obliterate Broncos 46-20 at Suncorp in Round 26 opener
stories.why_it_matters: Melbourne Storm handed the Brisbane Broncos a 46-20 hiding right in their own backyard at Suncorp Stadium on Thursday night. That's a massive win for Melbourne in a crucial Round 26 clash with finals implications. For any Broncos fans on the Gold Coast, it's a tough watch. The Storm look ominous heading into finals season.

stories.title: NRL's new kick-off rule trial — history made, but a flaw already found
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL's experimental kick-off rule trial made history during Round 26, but Fox Sports reports analysts have already spotted a structural 'flaw' in the new format. The new kick-off system is designed to improve game flow, but the unintended consequence emerged almost immediately. Critics are calling it a 'protest' moment for the competition's rules committee. Worth watching as the finals approach and the trial continues.

stories.title: AFL finals: Coach contract dramas loom as finals picture sharpens
stories.why_it_matters: With the AFL finals about to begin, columnist Callum Barrett writes that the real off-field drama is coach contract negotiations — several clubs have coaches out of contract at season's end, and the 'staring contests' between clubs and coaches are about to get very public. SuperCoach AFL Finals also kicks off this week, with the wildcard round now live for fantasy coaches.

stories.title: Matildas bracing for a sellout — extra seats in demand
stories.why_it_matters: The Matildas' upcoming match is on track to sell out, with fans urged to 'come out in droves.' The question is whether extra seats will be released to meet demand. Women's football continues to grow rapidly in Australia following the 2023 World Cup boost — the fact that sellout concerns are even a conversation reflects how far the sport has come.

stories.title: US Open: Women's contenders to watch beyond the top seeds
stories.why_it_matters: The US Open tennis is underway and the women's draw is wide open. Beyond the top seeds, a number of contenders are generating attention as dark horse picks. The tournament is always worth following for Australian fans, with several Australians in the draw and plenty of Grand Slam drama ahead.
